title: A king who knew not Joseph (Exodus 1:8–14)
word: A king who knew not Joseph
hook: a new Pharaoh, fear of a growing people, and slavery

segments.voice: Yesterday, chazak: Genesis ended with a coffin in Egypt, and the whole room saying be strong. Your line was be strong, be strong. This week took us from brothers bowing for bread, through the cup, Judah's plea and I am Joseph, to the end of a book. Today, a new one opens. Day seventy-seven.

The second book of the Torah is called Shemot, Names, because it opens by listing the names of Jacob's sons who came down to Egypt. Seventy people. Then Joseph dies, and all his brothers, and that whole generation. And their children have children, and the text piles up the words: they were fruitful, they swarmed, they multiplied, they grew very strong, and the land was filled with them. A family has become a people. Then one short verse turns everything: "Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who knew not Joseph." Today: what a man who forgets can do.
screen: `SHEMOT: NAMES.` → `SEVENTY BECOME A PEOPLE.` → `A NEW KING OVER EGYPT.`

segments.voice: Who knew not Joseph. How could a Pharaoh not know the man who saved Egypt from famine? The Talmud records two answers. One rabbi says: it really was a new king. The other says: it was the same king, who made new decrees, and acted as if he'd never known Joseph. Forgetting on purpose. Then listen to his speech to his people. The children of Israel are too many and too mighty for us. "Come, let us deal wisely with them," in case there's a war, and they join our enemies. Notice what's happened. Nobody has done anything. There's no crime, no rebellion. There's only a number, and a fear of what that number might do someday. And from fear comes a plan. First, taskmasters and forced labor: they build the store cities of Pithom and Raamses. Then the Torah says something almost defiant: "But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied." And the Egyptians, the text says, came to dread them. So the labor gets harder. Mortar, brick, work in the fields, all of it made bitter. This is how the whole story of the Exodus begins. Not with a monster. With a man who forgot what someone had done for his country, looked at a group of neighbors, and saw a threat. Jews tell this story every year at the Passover seder, and teachers have long noticed how ordinary its first step is. Forgetting. Then fear. Then cruelty that feels, to the people doing it, like being wise.
screen: `A NEW KING, OR ONE WHO CHOSE TO FORGET?` · `TOO MANY AND TOO MIGHTY FOR US.` · `LET US DEAL WISELY WITH THEM.` · `THE MORE THEY AFFLICTED, THE MORE THEY GREW.` · then, large: `FEAR FORGETS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where fear turns into cruelty. Settle, and breathe. Think about the last time you heard someone talk about a group of people as a threat. Too many of them. They'll take over. Maybe you heard it on the news. Maybe you've thought it. Notice what the fear was based on. Something they did, or something someone imagined they might do? You don't have to settle anything. Just see the first step. The bell holds the time.
A king who knew not Joseph. A new Pharaoh forgets what Joseph did for Egypt, fears a growing people, and makes them slaves.
screen: `A KING WHO KNEW NOT JOSEPH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: fear forgets. Today, when you feel afraid of a group of people, stop and remember one good thing someone from that group has done. Day seventy-seven.

howItsDone: The book of Exodus, Shemot in Hebrew, begins its synagogue reading each winter, and its story of slavery and freedom is retold at the Passover seder every spring.

fork.setup: you're Pharaoh's advisor. a foreign people in your land is growing fast. they've done nothing wrong. Pharaoh asks what to do.
options: welcome them; their ancestor saved Egypt.
deal wisely with them before they grow stronger.
fork.reveal: Pharaoh chooses "come, let us deal wisely with them": taskmasters, forced labor, and slavery. fear, dressed up as wisdom.

original.note: Hebrew: names. the Hebrew title of the book of Exodus, from its opening words.

trapdoor: what you thought: a new king who never heard of Joseph.
what it means: a king who forgot, or chose to forget, and turned fear of neighbors into slavery.
what a scholar hears: Sotah 11a: Rav and Shmuel disagree: a truly new king, or the same king with new decrees. Rashi on 1:8 cites both.
